items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The shellfish-and-mixed-fabrics comparison isolates divine capacity and legislative selectivity, contrasting explicit prohibitions of comparatively minor conduct with permissions to buy, beat, and bequeath human beings as property. Principal limitation: The argument exposes tension with perfect moral guidance, but dismissing historical context leaves unexamined whether regulation, covenantal scope, or gradual reform could distinguish these commands without denying the quoted permissions. Live burden: Dillahunty must demonstrate that contextual explanations cannot reconcile property ownership and punishment rules with a perfectly good lawgiver, while preserving his narrower conclusion that the Bible permits slavery rather than disproving every divine moral foundation.

items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The excerpt operationalizes impartiality through Rawls’s veil by asking participants to design arrangements without knowing whether they will be wealthy or poor, and supplements that test with universalization and willingness to correct mistakes. Principal limitation: These procedures expose self-serving perspectives, but the speaker acknowledges bias, incomplete information, and consequences, while offering no rule for resolving conflicts between fairness, well-being, universal adoption, and judgments about a better world. Live burden: The case must explain how conclusions reached behind the veil are compared and why correction tracks moral improvement rather than shifting conviction.
